introduction-escaping-the-cli-jungle.core: Running a multi-container app with docker run means long, error-prone commands for each container, network and volume. Docker Compose declares services, networks and volumes in one compose.yaml and manages them together (up, down, logs), making local development and integration testing reproducible.

first_principles.problem: New developers spend a day running ten docker run commands with the right flags to start the app locally.
truths: Local environments should match each other.

analogy.title: A recipe for a whole meal instead of separate instructions
analogy.story: One card says what to cook, in what order and how to serve it together.
analogy.breaks: Meals are eaten once; compose environments start and stop repeatedly.

example.title: Before and after
flow: Before: 10 docker run commands in a wiki
After: git clone && docker compose up

check.q: What's the main benefit of Docker Compose over docker run?
check.a: It declares a multi-container setup in one file and manages it with single commands.

the-compose-file-structure.core: A compose.yaml has top-level services (image or build, ports, environment, env_file, depends_on with health conditions, healthcheck, command, deploy resources), networks and volumes. Variables interpolate from .env, and multiple files merge (compose.yaml + compose.override.yaml) for local tweaks.

first_principles.problem: The API starts before the database is ready and crashes on boot.

analogy.title: A theatre production's cue sheet
analogy.story: Actors enter only when their cue (the healthy dependency) happens.
analogy.breaks: Actors can improvise; containers need explicit health checks to know when to start.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: API starts only after Postgres is ready.

code.text:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment: {DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres}
    depends_on:
      db: {condition: service_healthy}

check.q: How do you make a service wait until another is ready in Compose?
check.a: Add a healthcheck to the dependency and use depends_on with condition: service_healthy.

networking-in-compose.core: Compose creates a default network per project; services reach each other by service name via Docker's embedded DNS (db:5432), without publishing ports. ports publishes to the host for your browser or tools. Custom networks isolate groups (frontend/backend), and aliases or external networks connect to other projects.

first_principles.problem: Developers use localhost inside containers to reach the database and get connection refused.
truths: Each container has its own localhost.
Service names resolve on the project network.
Publishing is only for host access.

analogy.title: An office intranet with named desks
analogy.story: Colleagues reach each other by name internally; only the reception number is public.
analogy.breaks: Office phones work from anywhere; containers only resolve names on networks they've joined.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: web can't reach db directly; api bridges both.

check.q: Why doesn't 'localhost' work to reach another Compose service?
check.a: Each container has its own network namespace; localhost refers to itself, so use the service name.

volumes-persistent-storage-and-live-relo.core: Named volumes persist data (database files) across container recreation and are managed by Docker. Bind mounts map host directories into containers, enabling live code reloading during development. Compose Watch can sync or rebuild on file changes. Take care with node_modules and file permissions when bind-mounting.

first_principles.problem: Every docker compose down wipes the dev database, and code changes require rebuilding the image.
truths: Host files can be shared into containers.
Some dependencies shouldn't be overwritten by host files.
derivation: **down -v** only when you want a reset.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet that stays in the office versus a shared folder from home
analogy.story: The cabinet keeps records between staff changes; the shared folder shows edits instantly.
analogy.breaks: Shared folders sync both ways; bind mounts can overwrite container directories unexpectedly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Edits reload instantly; DB survives restarts.

code.text:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    command: npm run dev
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src
      - /app/node_modules
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
volumes:
  pgdata: {}

check.q: What does 'docker compose down -v' do that plain 'down' doesn't?
check.a: It also removes named volumes, deleting persisted data.

essential-compose-commands.core: Core commands: docker compose up -d (start), up --build (rebuild), down (stop and remove), ps, logs -f service, exec service sh (shell in a running container), run --rm service cmd (one-off tasks), config (render merged config), pull, restart and watch. Profiles (--profile) enable optional services.

first_principles.problem: Developers rebuild everything for every change and can't see why a service exited.
truths: One-off tasks shouldn't leave containers behind.

analogy.title: A TV remote for your whole stack
analogy.story: Power, volume, channel and info buttons for every container at once.
analogy.breaks: Remotes don't rebuild TVs; up --build does rebuild images.

code.text:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose exec api sh
docker compose run --rm api npm run migrate
docker compose --profile tools up -d pgadmin
docker compose down

check.q: What's the difference between 'compose exec' and 'compose run'?
check.a: exec runs a command in an existing running container; run starts a new container for a one-off command.
